content.text: We want to generate probabilistic artwork, efficiently. We are going to use random variables to make a picture filled with non-overlapping circles:
In our art, the circles are different sizes. Specifically, each circle's
radius

is drawn from a Pareto distribution (which is described below). The placement algorithm is greedy: we sample 1000 circle sizes. Sort them by size, largest to smallest. Loop over the circle sizes and place circles one by one.

To place a circle on the canvas, we sample the location of the center of the circle. Both the x and y coordinates are uniformly distributed over the dimensions of the canvas. Once we have selected a prospective location we then check if there would be a collision with a circle that has already been placed. If there is a collision we keep trying new locations until we find one that has no collisions.
The Pareto Distribution

There are many distributions that are ascetically pleasing! However, for many reasons there is something special about a Pareto distribution. In a Pareto distribution, there is a small chance of getting objects which are several orders of magnitude larger and a large probability of getting small objects. The Pareto distribution expresses a kind of mathematical self-similarity. No matter how far one zooms in or out, the shape of the distribution remains unchanged, a property known as
scale invariance

. This has a striking consequence: although small values dominate the landscape, the possibility of encountering something vastly larger never disappears. The probability of exceeding a value x decays only as a power,
, which makes the tail fall away slowly enough for extreme events to matter. In some regimes the extremes matter so much that even the average becomes undefined; when
, the mean itself is infinite. Such behavior sets the Pareto distribution apart from the more familiar, well-behaved distributions where moments neatly exist and extremes politely fade away.

On a log–log plot, the tail becomes a perfect straight line, the geometric signature of its power-law decay. The Pareto distribution thus distills a universe in which the commonplace is plentiful, the extraordinary is possible, and structure emerges from the balance between rarity and abundance.

Sampling from a Pareto Distribution
How can we draw samples from a Pareto? In python it's simple:
stats.pareto.rvs(a)

. In other programming languages, like JavaScript, it might not be that straightforward, so instead we can always use "inverse transform sampling". The idea is to sample a uniform random variable in the range (0, 1) and then select the value
